To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) the global buffer usage in update-caching is a strong function of data skew, and (2) in read-caching, the global buffer usage is a function of data skew and the number of nodes.

(a) the global buffer is most effective when there is no data skew among the multiple systems; (b) the global buffer usage increases with the skew, and (c) the global buffer can be used to reduce the number of invalidations, but the number of castouts increases with the skew.

(1) the use of a single global buffer can be very effective in reducing the communication overhead of multiple systems, and that (2) the effectiveness of the use of a common global buffer depends on the degree of data locality, which in turn, is determined by the workload characteristics.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions.
a study of the behavior of multiple systems coupled by a global buffer.
a performance study of a multiple system with a global buffer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a global buffer is a useful and cost-effective mechanism for coupling multiple systems, and it should be used whenever it is possible to do so.
, for all workloads and all system sizes, the use of a read-caching global buffer is the best approach.
, in a multiple-system setting, the global buffer can be used to improve performance significantly.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, in the absence of data skew, the use of a large global buffer is beneficial, but as data skew increases, the benefit of the global buffer diminishes.
the global buffer is a useful tool in reducing cross-invalidation and castout traffic in the multiple system environment, and the update-caching is a good design alternative to read-caching.

, with the update-caching scheme, the global buffer is a useful tool for improving the performance of a loosely coupled multiprocessor system with a shared memory, but the performance gain is highly dependent on the degree of data locality and data skew.
The main takeaway from our work is that

a global buffer is useful in reducing the number of page writes and cross-invalidations, thereby improving performance, and that read-caching is a better approach than the update-caching for the use of the global buffer in a multiple-system environment.
the use of a shared buffer is not necessarily the best choice in all situations.
the use of a single global buffer can be beneficial to a multiple-system environment in terms of performance.
